summary:
AstroMuscle is a logging app created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It infers, without diagnosing, the risk of muscle atrophy in astronauts on long-duration missions. In microgravity, muscle loses size, strength and endurance. According to NASA, on missions of about six months, leg strength drops by about 10–15%, even with daily exercise (Strock et al., 2023).

The app uses equipment already aboard the Space Station:

•	SLAMMD: body mass
•	ARED: squat load
•	Dynamometer: grip strength
•	Forearm sEMG: team proposal

It also includes a daily symptom questionnaire. Each week, it compares the data with the astronaut's baseline and assigns a low (loss under 10%), moderate (10 to 19.9%) or high (20% or more) risk level. The high-risk threshold comes from Scott et al. (2023). If symptoms are severe, it issues a separate alert. Finally, it generates a report for the ground-based physician, who makes the diagnosis.
details:
ASTROMUSCLE PROJECT

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Functional prototype with simulated data

1. PROJECT DESCRIPTION

AstroMuscle is a web application that helps monitor muscle loss in astronauts on long-duration missions. Each week, it compares the astronaut's measurements with their own baseline and infers a muscle atrophy risk level: low, moderate or high. The application does not diagnose: its output supports the decisions of the ground-based physician, who makes the diagnosis. Our guiding principle is: "The app infers; the physician diagnoses."

2. THE PROBLEM

Microgravity reduces muscle size, strength and endurance (National Aeronautics and Space Administration [NASA], n.d.-b). On missions of about six months, lower-limb muscle cross-sectional area and strength decrease by approximately 10–15%, even with exercise countermeasures (Strock et al., 2023), and some crew members return with losses greater than 10–20% in muscle strength and endurance (Rivas et al., 2023). Body mass decreases by 2–5% during the first month of flight (Smith et al., 2014). In a study of 46 astronauts with stays of 178 ± 48 days aboard the International Space Station (2011–2017), up to 17% were estimated to be at risk of performance-limiting deconditioning, using a 20% loss as the high-risk threshold (Scott et al., 2023). Today, these data are recorded on separate devices, so muscle loss can be detected late.

3. USERS AND SCOPE

The application has two users: the astronaut, who enters the data, and the ground-based physician, who receives the report and makes the diagnosis. Its objective is to provide a structured log and an early warning of negative trends, so that the medical team can prioritize clinical evaluation. Clinical diagnosis, the prescription of countermeasures and real-time connection to Space Station hardware are outside its scope.

4. EQUIPMENT AND DATA SOURCES

The application uses equipment already aboard the International Space Station.

Body mass (kg) is measured with SLAMMD, the Space Linear Acceleration Mass Measurement Device. Because scales do not work in microgravity, the astronaut holds onto the device, springs apply a known force, and the device measures the resulting acceleration; mass is calculated with Newton's second law, F = m · a (Rajulu et al., n.d.; Smith et al., 2014).

Maximum squat load (kg) is measured with ARED, the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device, which uses vacuum cylinders and a flywheel to reproduce weight-lifting loads in weightlessness (NASA, n.d.-a). The astronaut records the maximum load reached, always with the same exercise.

Maximum grip strength (kgf) is measured with a handgrip dynamometer: the astronaut squeezes as hard as possible for a few seconds and the peak value is recorded. Grip strength has already been measured aboard the Space Station (Puglia et al., 2018). One kilogram-force equals about 9.81 newtons.

Forearm surface electromyography (sEMG, in mV) is a team proposal: skin electrodes over the forearm muscles record electrical activity during maximal grip, and the RMS (root mean square) amplitude of the signal is reported. It is recorded only and is not used to classify risk.

The team recommends using the same exercise, limb and posture in every session. In the prototype, all values are entered manually.

5. DAILY QUESTIONNAIRE

Every day, the astronaut completes a two- to three-minute questionnaire: mission day, exercise time (0 to 6 hours), exercises performed on ARED, overall health (1 to 5), fatigue, muscle weakness, and muscle or joint pain (each from 0 to 10), and whether they noticed any drastic change (yes or no). The ARED exercises recorded are the squat (quadriceps, gluteals and hamstrings), the deadlift (lower back, gluteals and hamstrings), the heel raise (calves) and the bench press (chest, front shoulders and triceps). Only the squat is used in the risk calculation; the other exercises are recorded as training performed.

6. HOW THE RISK IS CALCULATED

For each weekly measurement, the application calculates the percentage change between the most recent week and the first recorded week (the baseline): change (%) = (current value − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100.

For squat load and grip strength, a loss of less than 10% is low risk, a loss of 10 to 19.9% is moderate risk, and a loss of 20% or more is high risk. The 10% cut-off is based on the 10–15% loss reported by NASA (Strock et al., 2023), and the 20% cut-off is the high-risk threshold of Scott et al. (2023).

The overall level is the higher of the squat load level and the grip strength level.

Body mass is supporting data (less than 2% low, 2 to 5% moderate, more than 5% high) and does not change the overall level, because body weight also changes with water and fat. sEMG does not change the level either, because there is no published reference threshold for it.

With fewer than two recorded weeks, the application shows "Not enough data".

Symptom alert: the application reviews the last seven mission days. If the astronaut reported any drastic change, or if average fatigue or weakness is 7 or higher, it raises a separate alert for the physician. This alert does not change the risk level. A drastic change also triggers an immediate alert when it is entered (simulated in the prototype).

The exact cut-off points and the symptom threshold of 7 out of 10 were set by the team and have not been clinically validated.

7. APPLICATION FEATURES

The application has four tabs. Daily contains the questionnaire. Weekly records the four measurements. Log shows the history of entries with their percentage change and lets the user delete entries or restore the sample data. Inference shows the risk level with an animated bar, the reasons, the details of each measurement, the symptom summary and a report for the physician that can be copied or marked as sent. From this tab, the data can be exported as JSON (full backup that can be imported again), CSV (tables for spreadsheets) or TXT (report), and a JSON file can be imported after the app checks it and the user confirms.

8. TECHNOLOGY

The application is a single HTML file written in HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with no external libraries or frameworks. It runs entirely in the browser, with no server or installation. Data is stored only on the user's device using the browser's localStorage, and no data leaves the device. The design uses a high-contrast monochrome style inspired by the Starlink app, the Barlow typeface from Google Fonts, straight frames with no rounded corners, and a background photograph of the Space Station over Earth with slow movement and twinkling stars. Risk colors are green for low, yellow for moderate and orange-red for high. The app includes accessibility features (labels on every field, keyboard navigation, screen-reader announcements and support for reduced-motion settings) and escapes all text before displaying it. It was tested with no layout errors at screen widths from 360 to 1366 pixels. It is available in Spanish and English and is published on GitHub Pages.

9. TESTING AND RESULTS

All test data are simulated. The baseline (week 1) is a body mass of 78.0 kg, grip strength of 46.0 kgf, ARED load of 80.0 kg and sEMG of 1.20 mV. At week 10 (75.7 kg, 41.4 kgf, 74.0 kg, 1.02 mV), the app correctly inferred moderate risk (grip −10.0%, ARED −7.5%, mass −2.9%). At week 24 (75.1 kg, 36.4 kgf, 68.0 kg, 0.95 mV), it correctly inferred high risk (grip −20.9%, ARED −15.0%, mass −3.7%, sEMG −20.8%). On day 70, a fatigue score of 7 correctly triggered the symptom alert without changing the risk level. A file exported from the Spanish version was correctly imported into the English version.

10. LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The data are simulated and the app has not been tested with astronauts. The thresholds are based on published studies but have not been clinically validated. For grip strength, changes smaller than about 4 kg may be due to measurement error (Abe et al., 2025), and the minimal clinically important difference is 5.0 to 6.5 kg (Bohannon, 2019). Data entry is manual, sEMG is recorded only, and NASA references are group averages, not individual values. Our next steps are to validate the thresholds with space medicine specialists, connect the app directly to SLAMMD, ARED, the dynamometer and sEMG, and test it with real training data.

13. CREDITS

The AstroMuscle team, with support from Claude (Anthropic), an artificial intelligence assistant, in creating the app code. Background images were provided by the team. This project was developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026; it does not use the NASA logo and does not represent the agency.
